newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China throws out dissident on visit to mother.
newsitem.headline: China throws out dissident on visit to mother.

text.p: A Chinese dissident who went into exile in Britain after the 1989 Tiananmen Square military crackdown in Beijing said on Friday he was expelled from China when he returned to visit his mother this week.
Liu Hongbin told Reuters in Hong Kong that police in Shanghai accused him of "activities incompatible with his tourist status" and ordered him to leave the country on Wednesday.
"I'm only a poet," he said, protesting that the action of the Chinese government was "absurd". "My hopes for China were ruined by the rude treatment I received," he said.
Liu, a poet who wrote pro-democracy poems during the crushed 1989 student democracy movement in the Chinese capital, left the eastern Chinese city for the British colony on Thursday morning.

The dissident poet, who holds a British passport, said he returned to visit his mother in the northern city of Qingdao five weeks ago on a tourist visa, and during his stay there he was harassed by security officials.
Liu said Qingdao police seized his British passport and only returned it a week later when he threatened he would travel to Beijing to get a new one from the British embassy.
He was also told not to make contact with any politically sensitive persons or to incite political activities.
Liu believed his expulsion was due to tighter control by police in the aftermath of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping's death last month.
After more than four weeks under virtual house arrest, as police regularly knocked on his door, Liu travelled to Nanjing.
But police continued to harass him there and when he was in Shanghai he was jumped by a dozen plainclothes police on Wednesday, he said.
Liu said he was taken away for questioning and accused him of breaching his stay as a tourist.
The police confined him in a hotel behind Shanghai airport and put him on a flight to Hong Kong on Thursday morning.

Han Dongfang, a leader of the ill-fated 1989 student-led democracy movement, told Reuters last week there would be no repeat of that crackdown either in China or in Hong Kong after the territory reverts to Chinese control this July.
But Han said there would be pressure to conform, and dissidents-in-exile in Hong Kong should leave for other countries before the handover, in order to stay safe.
